lessons.title: Articles — Le, La, Les
lessons.explanation: French nouns have gender (masculine/feminine). Use 'le' for masculine nouns, 'la' for feminine nouns, and 'les' for plural nouns. Unlike English, every noun has a gender you must memorize.
examples: le livre (the book - masc.)
la maison (the house - fem.)
les enfants (the children - pl.)
le garçon (the boy)
la fille (the girl)
lessons.tip: When you learn a new noun, always learn it with its article: le chat, la chaise.

quiz.question: What is the article for 'maison' (house, feminine)?
Which article means 'the' for a plural noun?

lessons.title: Subject Pronouns — Je, Tu, Il, Elle…
lessons.explanation: French has six subject pronouns: je (I), tu (you-informal), il (he), elle (she), nous (we), vous (you-formal/plural), ils (they-masc.), elles (they-fem.).
examples: Je suis étudiant. (I am a student.)
Tu es mon ami. (You are my friend.)
Il parle français. (He speaks French.)
Nous aimons la musique. (We love music.)
lessons.tip: Use 'tu' with friends and family; use 'vous' with strangers, teachers, and elders.

quiz.question: How do you say 'I' in French?
Which pronoun would you use for 'we'?

lessons.title: Être — To Be
lessons.explanation: The verb 'être' (to be) is essential in French. It is irregular: je suis, tu es, il/elle est, nous sommes, vous êtes, ils/elles sont.
examples: Je suis français. (I am French.)
Elle est médecin. (She is a doctor.)
Nous sommes fatigués. (We are tired.)
Vous êtes gentils. (You are kind.)
lessons.tip: Être is used to describe identity, nationality, profession, and states.

quiz.question: How do you say 'she is' in French?
What does 'nous sommes' mean?

lessons.title: Avoir — To Have
lessons.explanation: The verb 'avoir' (to have) is another essential irregular verb: j'ai, tu as, il/elle a, nous avons, vous avez, ils/elles ont.
examples: J'ai un chien. (I have a dog.)
Tu as une sœur? (Do you have a sister?)
Il a faim. (He is hungry — lit. he has hunger.)
Nous avons une voiture. (We have a car.)
lessons.tip: Many expressions that use 'to be' in English use 'avoir' in French: avoir faim = to be hungry, avoir soif = to be thirsty.

quiz.question: How do you say 'I have' in French?
What does 'avoir faim' mean?

lessons.title: Regular -ER Verbs
lessons.explanation: Most French verbs end in -ER and follow a regular pattern. Remove -ER and add: -e, -es, -e, -ons, -ez, -ent. Example: parler (to speak) → je parle, tu parles, il parle, nous parlons, vous parlez, ils parlent.
examples: Je parle français. (I speak French.)
Tu manges une pomme. (You eat an apple.)
Elle habite à Paris. (She lives in Paris.)
Nous aimons voyager. (We love to travel.)
lessons.tip: The je, il, and ils/elles forms sound the same for -ER verbs even though they're spelled differently.

quiz.question: What is the 'nous' form of 'parler'?
What ending does 'tu' take for -ER verbs?

lessons.title: Adjective Agreement
lessons.explanation: In French, adjectives must agree in gender and number with the noun they describe. Usually add -e for feminine and -s for plural. Example: grand (big, masc.) → grande (fem.) → grands (masc. pl.) → grandes (fem. pl.).
examples: un garçon grand (a tall boy)
une fille grande (a tall girl)
des garçons grands (tall boys)
Elle est intelligente. (She is intelligent.)
lessons.tip: Most adjectives come AFTER the noun in French, unlike in English.

quiz.question: How do you make 'petit' (small) feminine?
Where do most adjectives go in French?
options: at the end of the sentence

lessons.title: Possessive Adjectives
lessons.explanation: French possessive adjectives (mon/ma/mes, ton/ta/tes, son/sa/ses, notre/nos, votre/vos, leur/leurs) agree with the gender and number of the noun possessed, not the possessor. Before a feminine noun starting with a vowel sound, use 'mon/ton/son' instead of 'ma/ta/sa' for smoother pronunciation.
examples: mon frère (my brother)
ma sœur (my sister)
son amie (his/her friend — fem. starting with a vowel, uses 'son')
leurs enfants (their children)
lessons.tip: The possessive agrees with the noun that follows, not the gender of the owner — 'son livre' can mean his or her book.

quiz.question: Which possessive is used before 'amie' (fem., starts with a vowel) meaning 'his/her'?
Does 'son' always mean 'his' in French?

lessons.title: Comparatives and Superlatives
lessons.explanation: French comparatives use plus/moins...que (more/less...than) or aussi...que (as...as). Superlatives use le/la/les + plus/moins + adjective. Bon (good) has the irregular comparative meilleur (better).
examples: Elle est plus grande que moi. (She is taller than me.)
Ce livre est aussi intéressant que l'autre. (This book is as interesting as the other.)
C'est le plus grand bâtiment de la ville. (It's the tallest building in the city.)
Ce gâteau est meilleur que l'autre. (This cake is better than the other.)
lessons.tip: Remember 'bon → meilleur' is irregular; don't say 'plus bon.'

quiz.question: How do you say 'more...than' in French?
What is the irregular comparative of 'bon'?

lessons.title: Passé Composé — Past Tense
lessons.explanation: The passé composé is the main past tense for completed actions. It uses avoir or être + past participle. Most verbs use avoir; verbs of motion and reflexive verbs use être.
examples: J'ai mangé une pizza. (I ate a pizza.)
Elle est allée au marché. (She went to the market.)
Nous avons vu ce film. (We saw that film.)
Il est arrivé hier. (He arrived yesterday.)
lessons.tip: Verbs using être in passé composé: aller, venir, partir, arriver, naître, mourir, and reflexive verbs.

quiz.question: Which auxiliary is used with 'aller' in passé composé?
What is the past participle of 'manger' (to eat)?

lessons.title: Imparfait — Imperfect Tense
lessons.explanation: The imparfait describes ongoing, habitual, or background past actions and descriptions, unlike the passé composé which marks completed events. It is formed from the 'nous' present stem plus endings: -ais, -ais, -ait, -ions, -iez, -aient. Être is irregular (ét-).
examples: Quand j'étais petit, je jouais dehors. (When I was little, I used to play outside.)
Il faisait beau ce jour-là. (It was nice weather that day.)
Nous habitions à Lyon. (We used to live in Lyon.)
Elle lisait pendant que je cuisinais. (She was reading while I was cooking.)
lessons.tip: Take the 'nous' form of the present tense, drop -ons, and add the imparfait endings — this works for almost every verb except être.

quiz.question: What is the imparfait stem derived from?
What is the 'je' imparfait form of 'être'?

lessons.title: Reflexive (Pronominal) Verbs
lessons.explanation: French reflexive verbs use a reflexive pronoun (me, te, se, nous, vous, se) that matches the subject and is placed before the conjugated verb. Common reflexives: se lever, se laver, s'habiller. In the passé composé, reflexive verbs always use être, and the participle often agrees with the subject.
examples: Je me lève à sept heures. (I get up at seven.)
Elle se lave les mains. (She washes her hands.)
Nous nous habillons vite. (We get dressed quickly.)
Ils se sont couchés tard. (They went to bed late.)
lessons.tip: In passé composé, reflexive verbs always take être, and the past participle usually agrees with the subject in gender and number.

quiz.question: Which auxiliary do reflexive verbs use in passé composé?
What pronoun goes with 'nous' in reflexive verbs?

lessons.title: Futur Simple — Future Tense
lessons.explanation: The futur simple expresses future actions, formed by adding endings (-ai, -as, -a, -ons, -ez, -ont) directly to the infinitive (dropping the final -e for -re verbs). Many common verbs have irregular stems: être→ser-, avoir→aur-, aller→ir-, faire→fer-.
examples: Je parlerai avec elle demain. (I will speak with her tomorrow.)
Tu seras content. (You will be happy.)
Nous aurons le temps. (We will have time.)
Ils iront en France l'été prochain. (They will go to France next summer.)
lessons.tip: The futur simple endings are identical to the present tense of 'avoir' (ai, as, a, ons, ez, ont) — that makes them easy to remember.

quiz.question: What is the 'je' futur simple form of 'parler'?
What is the irregular future stem of 'être'?

lessons.title: Le Subjonctif — Subjunctive Mood
lessons.explanation: The subjunctive expresses doubt, wish, emotion, necessity, or uncertainty. It is used after expressions like 'il faut que', 'je veux que', 'bien que'. Formation: take ils-form of present, remove -ent, add: -e, -es, -e, -ions, -iez, -ent.
examples: Il faut que tu viennes. (You must come.)
Je veux qu'elle soit heureuse. (I want her to be happy.)
Bien qu'il fasse froid, nous sortons. (Although it is cold, we are going out.)
Il est important que vous étudiiez. (It is important that you study.)
lessons.tip: The subjunctive almost always appears in a subordinate clause after 'que'.

quiz.question: Which expression triggers the subjunctive?

lessons.title: Le Conditionnel — Conditional Mood
lessons.explanation: The conditional expresses hypothetical actions ('would') or polite requests, formed with the same stem as the futur simple plus the imparfait endings (-ais, -ais, -ait, -ions, -iez, -aient). It is used in the result clause of hypothetical 'si' sentences (si + imparfait, conditionnel).
examples: Je voudrais un café, s'il vous plaît. (I would like a coffee, please.)
Si j'avais de l'argent, je voyagerais. (If I had money, I would travel.)
Elle serait heureuse de vous voir. (She would be happy to see you.)
Pourriez-vous m'aider? (Could you help me?)
lessons.tip: Conditionnel = futur stem + imparfait endings. Use it after 'si + imparfait' for hypothetical situations.

quiz.question: What stem does the conditional use?
In 'Si j'avais de l'argent, je voyagerais,' which clause is in the conditional?

lessons.title: Relative Pronouns — qui, que, dont, où
lessons.explanation: Relative pronouns connect clauses and replace a noun. Qui = subject (who/which). Que = direct object (whom/that/which). Dont = replaces 'de + noun' (whose/of which). Où = place or time (where/when).
examples: L'homme qui parle est mon père. (The man who is speaking is my father.)
Le livre que je lis est intéressant. (The book that I am reading is interesting.)
C'est le film dont je t'ai parlé. (It's the movie I told you about.)
C'est la ville où je suis né. (It's the city where I was born.)
lessons.tip: Qui is followed directly by a verb (it's the subject); que is followed by a subject + verb (it's the object).

quiz.question: Which relative pronoun replaces 'de + noun'?
Which relative pronoun acts as the subject of the relative clause?

lessons.title: Le Plus-que-parfait — Pluperfect
lessons.explanation: The plus-que-parfait describes an action that happened before another past action ('had done'), formed with the imparfait of avoir or être plus the past participle. It follows the same auxiliary and agreement rules as the passé composé.
examples: J'avais déjà mangé quand elle est arrivée. (I had already eaten when she arrived.)
Elle était partie avant notre arrivée. (She had left before our arrival.)
Nous avions fini le travail. (We had finished the work.)
Ils s'étaient couchés tôt. (They had gone to bed early.)
lessons.tip: Plus-que-parfait = imparfait of avoir/être + past participle — think of it as 'one step further back' than passé composé.

quiz.question: What auxiliary tense is used to form the plus-que-parfait?
What does the plus-que-parfait express?
options: an action before another past action
